source.title: Progresses on Some Open Problems Related to Infinitely Many Symmetries

accepted.question_text: How can one give concrete physical interpretations for the infinitely many symmetries and conservation laws that arise in integrable systems, beyond the small subset that already have familiar interpretations such as space-time translation invariance, Galilean or Lorentz invariance, scaling invariance, and the conservation laws for mass, momentum, and energy?

For nonlinear physical systems described by partial differential equations and therefore having infinitely many degrees of freedom, are the currently known infinitely many symmetries complete, or are there additional undiscovered symmetries beyond the standard known families?

Can generalized symmetries, especially generalized local symmetries rather than only Lie point symmetries or nonlocal symmetry constraints, be used to derive exact multi-wave solutions of integrable partial differential equation systems, particularly multi-soliton solutions and other exact solutions beyond single periodic cnoidal waves, solitary waves, and Painleve-type solutions?

For integrable systems with infinitely many generalized symmetries of varying order, why do certain expected orders appear to be absent, and more generally do even-order or fractional-order generalized symmetries exist for standard integrable equations such as KdV and modified KdV?

Given a particular solution u0(x,t) of a system, can the action of infinitely many symmetries introduce an infinite sequence of arbitrary constants into that specific solution, extending the familiar use of spatial and temporal translation symmetries to introduce constants such as x0 and t0?
